```{r include = FALSE}

# This document was written in R Version 4.2.0, RMarkdown version 2.12
# The OSF Page for the original paper is: https://osf.io/fpsu8/
# The original paper: https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797619826972

# Packages
library(pwr)     # Version 1.3-0
library(MASS)    # Version 7.3-57
library(wmwpow)  # Version 0.1.3
library(MKpower) # Version 0.5
library(psych)   # Version 2.2.5
library(knitr)   # Version 1.37

# Read data from OSF page
data <- read.csv("https://osf.io/e734d/download", skip = 1)
```

Vardy & Atkinson (2019) describes a pair of dictator-game experiments conducted within two villages — one considered Christian and the other considered Kastom — before and after Cyclone Pam. The games required participants to allocate 10 coins to people among four conditions:

1. Someone in their own village or someone in another village of the same religion
2. Themselves or someone in another village of the same religion
3. Someone in another village of the same religion or someone in a village of a different religion
4. Themselves or someone in a village of a different religion

Actual money would then be allocated based on their responses. The researchers also administered a questionnaire to assess how the participants had been affected by the cyclone. The OSF page for this paper provides the data for participants who could be contacted following the cyclone, as well as the script for the game and questionnaire. No code is provided.

# Sample

## Size

The post-hurricane sample size can be replicated. The full pre-cyclone sample cannot be replicated because the full sample data is not provided.

```{r echo = FALSE}
# Create table of sample size by sex and site
kable(table(data$Sex, data$Site), 
      caption = "Sex by Site")
```

## Age Mean and Standard Deviation

The mean and standard deviation of the sample ages can be replicated, with the exception of the mean age of the overall sample. In the paper this is reported as 38.51, but the mean() function as applied to the data returns 37.51.

```{r echo = FALSE}
# Mean and SD of ages for both sites
m_all  <- round(mean(data$pre_age), 2) # 37.51
sd_all <- round(sd(data$pre_age), 2)   # 15.49

# Mean and SD of ages for Christian sites
m_chr  <- round(mean(data$pre_age[data$Site == "Christian"]), 2) # 36.25
sd_chr <- round(sd(data$pre_age[data$Site == "Christian"]), 2)   # 14.80

# Mean and SD of ages for Kastom sites
m_kas  <- round(mean(data$pre_age[data$Site == "Kastom"]), 2) # 39.54
sd_kas <- round(sd(data$pre_age[data$Site == "Kastom"]), 2)   # 16.46

# Table of mean and SD of ages
kable(data.frame("Group" = c("Overall", "Christian", "Kastom"),
           "Mean"  = c(m_all, m_chr, m_kas),
	         "SD"    = c(sd_all, sd_chr, sd_kas)), 
      caption = "Age by Group")
```

## Power
In the paper, it is stated that the sample had at least 80% power to detect effects equal to a Wilcoxin Signed Rank effect size of 0.2 This cannot be replicated; the paper uses a Paired Wilcoxin Test, but base R does not have a function for this analysis and if a package is used it is not specified in the paper. The package `wmwpow' does allow for the calculation of power for Wilcoxin tests, but only for one or two sided tests.

# Results

## Cyclone-Affectedness Measures
The paper reports the responses to the questionnaire items regarding how participants were affected by the cyclone. These can be replicated by dividing the number of positive responses by the number of rows in the dataset.

```{r echo = FALSE}
# Homes
mea_dam <- round(nrow(data[data$DAMAGE == 1, ]) / nrow(data) * 100, 2)   # 85.37
mea_rel <- round(nrow(data[data$RELOCATE == 1, ]) / nrow(data) * 100, 2) # 80.49
mea_inj <- round(nrow(data[data$INJURE == 1, ]) / nrow(data) * 100, 2)   # 17.07
mea_dif <- round(nrow(data[data$DIFMONEY == 1, ]) / nrow(data) * 100, 2) # 75
mea_foo <- round(nrow(data[data$FOODAID == 1, ]) / nrow(data) * 100, 2)  # 85.37

# Table
kable(data.frame("Measure" = c("Damage", "Relocation", "Injury", 
                               "Dif Money", "Food Aid"),
           "Percentage" = c(mea_dam, mea_rel, mea_inj, mea_dif, mea_foo)), 
      caption = "Cyclone-Affectedness")
```

## Principal Component Analysis
```{r include = FALSE}
# Filter data to columns 37 to 52, with rows missing values removed
data_filt <- na.omit(data[colnames(data)[37:52]])

# PCA using filtered data, with 4 factors and an oblimin rotation
# Note: Requires the package "GPArotation"
data_pca <- principal(data_filt, nfactors = 4, rotate = "oblimin")

# Create Dataframe of loadings for PCA
pca_loadings <- data.frame("VAR" = colnames(data)[37:52], 
                           "DAMAGE"  = round(data_pca$loadings[,1], 2), 
                           "NEED"  = round(data_pca$loadings[,2], 2), 
                           "ALLINJ"  = round(data_pca$loadings[,3], 2), 
                           "HEARCRY"  = round(data_pca$loadings[,4], 2))

# Reset index
rownames(pca_loadings) <- NULL
```

A principal component analysis involving 4 components was conducted on the measures and reported in the paper. Using the principal() function from the psych package, I was able to replicate the loadings and reliabilities reported in the paper.

```{r echo = FALSE}
# Factor Names
f_names <- c("Damage to Property", "Need for Resource Aid", 
             "Injury to Self and Loved Ones", "Exposure to Others in Distress")

# Factor Reliabilities
f_rel_1 <- alpha(data[, c("DAMAGE", "RELOCATE", "SHELTER", "STAY")])$total[1, 1]
f_rel_2 <- alpha(data[, c("MONEYASS", "DIFMONEY", "FOODAID", "DEPINJ")])$total[1, 1]
f_rel_3 <- alpha(data[, c("FAMINJ", "FAMDEAD", "INJURE")])$total[1, 1]
f_rel_4 <- alpha(data[, c("RESCUE", "FAMFEAR", "HEARCRY")])$total[1, 1]

# PCA
data_pca <- principal(data[, 37:52], nfactors = 4, rotate = "oblimin")

# Factor Eigenvalues
f_eig <- data_pca$values[1:4]

# Factor Variance
f_var <- data_pca$Vaccounted[2, 1:4]

# Create dataframe
pca_results <- data.frame("Factor" = f_names, 
                          "Reliability" = c(f_rel_1, f_rel_2, f_rel_3, f_rel_4), 
                          "Eigenvalues" = f_eig, 
                          "Variance" = f_var)

# Round results to two decimal places
pca_results[2:4] <- round(pca_results[2:4], 2)

# Reset Index
row.names(pca_results) <- NULL

kable(pca_results, 
      caption = "Principal Component Analysis")
```

Loadings:

- Damage to Property: had to relocated (`r pca_loadings[7, 2]`); home was damaged (`r pca_loadings[6, 2]`); stayed somewhere other than their home (`r pca_loadings[1, 2]`); needed shelter (`r pca_loadings[3, 2]`); loss of belongings (`r pca_loadings[8, 2]`)
- Need for Resource Aid: needed financial assistance (`r pca_loadings[5, 3]`); experienced financial difficulties (`r pca_loadings[4, 3]`); needed food and water aid (`r pca_loadings[2, 3]`); dependent on others following injury (`r pca_loadings[10, 3]`)
- Injury to Self and Loved Ones: Family injury (`r pca_loadings[11, 4]`); Family dead (`r pca_loadings[14, 4]`); injury (`r pca_loadings[9, 4]`); family dependence (`r pca_loadings[12, 4]`)
- Exposure: Rescue (`r pca_loadings[15, 5]`); family fear (`r pca_loadings[13, 5]`); hear cry (`r pca_loadings[16, 5]`); family dependence (`r pca_loadings[12, 5]`)

## Wilcoxin Tests
Four Wilcoxin Signed Rank tests were conducted. Of these, three can be replicated using the wilcox.test() function. The test for allocations to a participant's village or a different village of the same religion cannot be replicated. In the paper, the W statistics for this test is given as 2843.5, with a p value of .323; I can only get a W statistic of 2864.5.

\newpage

```{r echo = FALSE}

# Names
wilcox_names <- c("Co-Religionists vs. Self", 
                  "Outgroup vs. Self", 
                  "Outgroup vs. Co-Religionists", 
                  "Co-Religionists vs. Own Village")

# Wilcoxin Tests
w_co_s <- wilcox.test(data$pre.Corel..v.Self.,  # V=4251
                      data$post.Corel..v.Self., # p=.01
                      paired = TRUE)

w_o_s <- wilcox.test(data$pre.Outgroup..v.Self.,  # V=5063
                     data$post.Outgroup..v.Self., # p=.0007
                     paired = TRUE)

w_ou_co <- wilcox.test(data$pre.Outgroup..v.Corel., # V = 3543.5
                       data$post.Outgroup..v.Corel., # P = 0.014
                       paired = TRUE)

w_co_own <- wilcox.test(data$pre.Corel..v.Own.Village.,  # V=2864.5
                        data$post.Corel..v.Own.Village., # p=.323
                        paired = TRUE)

# V Values
wilcox_v <- c(w_co_s$statistic, w_o_s$statistic, w_ou_co$statistic, 
              w_co_own$statistic)

# P Values
wilcox_p <- c(w_co_s$p.value, w_o_s$p.value, w_ou_co$p.value, w_co_own$p.value)

wilcox_results <- data.frame("x" = wilcox_names, 
                             "y" = round(wilcox_v, 1), 
                             "z" = round(wilcox_p, 3))

kable(wilcox_results, 
      col.names = c("Comparison", "V Statistic", "P Value"), 
      caption = "Wilcoxin Tests")
```

## Chi-Square Tests
Four McNemar Chi-Square tests were conducted to check if game allocations changed for the same condition following the cyclone. I was able to replicate the results presented in the paper using the mcnemar.test() function.

```{r echo = FALSE}

# Names
chi_names <- c("Self Vs. Co-Religionist", "Self Vs. Outgroup", 
               "Co-Religionist Vs. Own Village", "Outgroup Vs. Co-Religionist")

# Self Vs. Co-Religionist
c_co_s <- mcnemar.test(data$pre.Corel..v.Self..binary,          # X = 3.0154
                       data$post.Corel..v.Self..binary)         # p = 0.08248

# Self Vs. Outgroup
c_ou_s <- mcnemar.test(data$pre.Outgroup..v.Self..binary,       # X = 11.161
                       data$post.Outgroup..v.Self..binary)      # p = 0.0008355

# Co-Religionist Vs. Own Village
c_ou_own <- mcnemar.test(data$pre.Corel..v.Own.Village..binary,   # X = 0.94231
                         data$post.Corel..v.Own.Village..binary)  # p = 0.3317

# Outgroup Vs. Co-Religionist
c_o_co <-   mcnemar.test(data$pre.Outgroup..v.Corel..binary,      # X = 5.8226
                         data$post.Outgroup..v.Corel..binary)     # p = 0.01582

# X Values
chi_x <- c(c_co_s$statistic, c_ou_s$statistic, c_ou_own$statistic, 
           c_o_co$statistic)

# P Values
chi_p <- c(c_co_s$p.value, c_ou_s$p.value, c_ou_own$p.value, c_o_co$p.value)

chi_results <- data.frame("x" = chi_names, 
                          "y" = round(chi_x, 2), 
                          "z" = round(chi_p, 3))

kable(chi_results, 
      col.names = c("Comparison", "X Statistic", "P Value"), 
      caption = "Chi-Square Tests")
```

## Change
Figure 5 in the paper displays the direction of change in allocations following the cyclone — whether participants gave more, less, or the same to one person (eg., themselves) in comparison to another (eg., a person in a different village of the same religion). Using the table() and prop.table() function on the columns for this change, I was able to replicate the figures in the paper.

```{r echo = FALSE}

# Co-Religionist Vs. Own Village
cha_co_ow <- data.frame(prop.table(table(data$net_corel1_ord))) 

# Co-Religionist Vs. Self
cha_co_s <- data.frame(prop.table(table(data$net_corel2_ord)))

# Outgroup Vs. Co-Religionist
cha_ou_co <- data.frame(prop.table(table(data$net_outgroup3_ord)))

# Outgroup Vs. Self
cha_ou_s <- data.frame(prop.table(table(data$net_outgroup4_ord)))

#change_data <- 

# Less
change_less <- c(cha_co_ow[1, 2], cha_co_s[1, 2], cha_ou_co[1, 2], cha_ou_s[1, 2])
change_more <- c(cha_co_ow[2, 2], cha_co_s[2, 2], cha_ou_co[2, 2], cha_ou_s[2, 2])
change_same <- c(cha_co_ow[3, 2], cha_co_s[3, 2], cha_ou_co[3, 2], cha_ou_s[3, 2])

#
change_results <- data.frame("v" = c("More", "Less", "Same"), 
                             "w" = round(c(change_less[1], change_more[1], change_same[1]), 3), 
                             "x" = round(c(change_less[2], change_more[2], change_same[2]), 3), 
                             "y" = round(c(change_less[3], change_more[3], change_same[3]), 3), 
                             "z" = round(c(change_less[4], change_more[4], change_same[4]), 3))
kable(change_results, 
      col.names = c("Change", "Co-Religionists vs. Own Village", 
                    "Co-Religionists vs. Self", 
                    "Outgroup vs. Co-Religionists", 
                    "Outgroup vs. Self"), 
      caption = "Change in Allocations")

```

## Logistic and Tobit Regression
To test whether the cyclone-affectnedness measures could explain variation in coin allocation, logistic and tobit regressions were carried out. These used the factors from the principal component analysis as independent variables, and precyclone allocation and village as control variables.

While I can conduct a logistic regression, a tobit regression is not something that I have done before and because no information is provided regarding how this was done or how the model was specified I have not attempted to replicate this.

I was not able to replicate any of the results of the logistic regressions presented in the paper.

\newpage

### Self vs. Co-Religionists
```{r echo = FALSE}
model_1 <- glm(formula = post.Corel..v.Self..binary ~ PROPDAM + NEED + INJURY + 
               FEAR + pre.Corel..v.Self..binary + as.factor(Site), 
               family = binomial, data = data)

summary(model_1)
```

\newpage

### Self vs. Outgroup
```{r echo = FALSE}
model_2 <- glm(formula = post.Outgroup..v.Self..binary ~ PROPDAM + NEED + INJURY +
               FEAR + pre.Outgroup..v.Self..binary + as.factor(Site), 
               family = binomial, data = data)

summary(model_2)
```

\newpage

### Own Village vs. Different Village of Same Religion
```{r echo = FALSE}
model_3 <- glm(formula = post.Corel..v.Own.Village..binary ~ PROPDAM + NEED + 
               INJURY + FEAR + pre.Corel..v.Own.Village..binary + 
               as.factor(Site), 
               family = binomial, data = data)

summary(model_3)
```

\newpage

```{r echo = FALSE}
model_4 <- glm(formula = post.Outgroup..v.Corel..binary ~ PROPDAM + NEED + 
               INJURY + FEAR + pre.Outgroup..v.Corel..binary +
```
